The core issue is subscription-related.

The subscription plan should be the source of truth for all plan-dependent logic. When no subscription exists, fall back to the workspace plan. The fix is to prefer subscription.plan over org.plan whenever resolving the effective plan.

Billing-service comments already treat subscription as the authority, but many places still read org.

changePlan and trial expiry may update subscription without syncing org.plan. listTrialsEndingBefore might include non-trialing subscriptions. Already-diverged records need readers to follow the subscription plan directly.

The burst limit uses setOrgPlan, which caches the plan in memory.

Stale org plans cause burst limits to stay free. Billing shows Growth but workspace acts like Free. Trial expiry updates the subscription to free while org.plan stays Growth, so features remain. Paid plans chosen during trial are incorrectly downgraded because listTrialsEndingBefore ignores the trialing status. Two fixes are needed.

listTrialsEndingBefore should only return trials with status "trialing". All plan consumers must read the subscription plan first, falling back to org.plan. The workspace switcher and header currently show Free because they use org.plan. Display logic also needs to read from the subscription.

Readers must resolve the effective plan from the subscription at read time, not only on write. The trial sweep will then correctly skip workspaces whose status has already become active. The job already handles trials that have outgrown Free limits.

The phrase "changes nothing more" likely means no additional downgrades occur, not that the job stops entirely. If a trial's status is never updated to active, the sweep would retry and fail again on every run. Marking already-downgraded trials as processed could prevent redundant attempts.

`setOrgPlan` is defined but may never be called.

Burst limits default to free unless `setOrgPlan` is called. Growth orgs remain throttled because the plan never gets updated after upgrade.

A single function that resolves the effective plan should be used throughout the organization.

The plan is used for both behavior and display across many pages and services. Subscription should be the single authority.

Export a `planFor` helper that returns `subscription.plan ?? org.plan`. Overlay the resolved plan when loading organizations for display. This fixes behavior and UI automatically across all readers without touching dozens of files.
The billing-plan-card component contains interesting logic.

The most robust fix is to overlay the subscription plan onto organization data when reading orgs.

The rate limiter defaults to free burst limits because no code calls setOrgPlan. This explains why upgraded workspaces still hit Free throttling after about 60 rapid comments.

The 60-comment burst limit matches the base bucket capacity. Growth plans would scale this to 6000. Overlaying the plan in the repository alone is insufficient because services never call setOrgPlan. The effective plan must be resolved and passed into consumeRateLimit from the three services.

The comment service currently skips loading the organization before rate limiting. A small `effectivePlan` helper in billing-service could resolve the plan and call `setOrgPlan` before each consume. Import cycles between rate-limit and repositories are unlikely. Actions also call `consumeRateLimit` directly before services.

Actions consume rate limits before services. If the action uses the free plan, it creates a bucket at free capacity. The service later setting the growth plan cannot fix this because the bucket state is already locked in. The limiter reads config.capacity on every call to refill, but the initial token count is fixed at creation time.

The rate limiter's refill logic does not instantly adopt a new plan's capacity. When the plan changes mid-bucket, the token count stays at the previous remaining balance if no time has elapsed since the last refill. The bucket therefore remains stuck at the old free limit until the next refill cycle.

The plan must be resolved at the exact moment of consumption, not from a stale cache. If the first request after an upgrade lands before the plan is set, the bucket initializes at free capacity and remains stuck there. The bug occurs when an organization upgrades but its first post still hits the old 60-comment burst limit.

Fixing plan lookup inside configFor would correct new buckets and existing ones that were nearly full when the free plan was active. A process-lifetime cache of tokens at the old capacity is itself a bug. When a plan increases, the bucket should immediately adopt the new capacity.

The cleanest fix is to key each rate-limit bucket by both organization and plan. When a workspace upgrades or downgrades, it receives a fresh bucket with the correct capacity immediately. This avoids stale token counts and eliminates the need to scale or reset existing buckets.

A `resolvePlan(orgId)` helper in billing-service can fetch the current plan directly inside `consumeRateLimit`. This removes the need for services to call `setOrgPlan` beforehand. Import cycles are unlikely because rate-limit would pull from repositories rather than billing-service.

The plan resolution helper will live directly inside `consumeRateLimit` rather than in billing-service. This lets both actions and services resolve the current plan automatically without any caller needing to call `setOrgPlan` first. Anonymous organizations for password resets correctly default to the free plan. The helper will read from the cache but always verify against the subscription repository to avoid trusting a stale cached value.

The plan resolver will skip caching entirely. A subscription row always overrides the organization plan, so a direct read from SQLite is sufficient and avoids stale limits.

Rate limit tests call setOrgPlan without a database.

Production never calls setOrgPlan, so it always falls back to the free default. That is the burst bug. Tests should prefer the database subscription when available, then fall back to the cache or org.plan.

The fix checks the cache first, then falls back to the database subscription and org plan. Existing rate-limit buckets keep their current token count after an upgrade, so they refill slowly rather than instantly. The refill rate is 200 tokens per minute.

The core issue is that limits remain at the Free tier after an upgrade. A burst immediately after upgrading still hits the old token count because the free bucket retains roughly 60 tokens. Keying by plan is a useful extra, but it does not fix the fundamental limit mismatch.
